project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car:
South Carolina is special to me because of its people. Everywhere I go I meet the same quiet strength, the same stubborn hope, the same love that keeps communities standing even when the systems around them fail. I’ve seen parents working two jobs still show up for their kids’ school events. I’ve watched neighbors share food when groceries ran thin. I’ve seen elders hold entire blocks together with wisdom and kindness. I’ve met young people fighting to build a future that feels bigger than their circumstances. When I volunteered with the homeless, mentored trans youth, or helped Korean elders navigate services, I saw people who refuse to give up on each other. South Carolina is full of beautiful people who open their doors, their kitchens, their hearts, even when they have little to spare. That kind of everyday courage shaped me. It taught me what community means and why it’s worth fighting for. The people here are not defined by struggle, they’re defined by the way they keep choosing their communities to raise their families in, and invest in. That’s what makes this place special to me.

I live in Columbia, and it is special to me because the people here carry a kind of resilience you can feel in your bones. This city has lived through reinvention after reinvention, from its role in the Civil War to the slow, stubborn rebuilding that followed, to the cultural crossroads it has become today. You can see that history on Main Street, in the old mills turned into apartments, in the churches that have stood through generations, and in the neighborhoods that hold stories most tourists never hear. What moves me most is the spirit of the people who call this place home. I’ve seen families on Decker, North Main, and Beltline keep their communities alive through pure grit. I’ve seen elders in Earlewood and Hollywood Hills carry decades of memory and still greet every new face with warmth. I’ve watched kids in Northeast Columbia dream big even when the odds lean hard against them. I’ve felt the pride of Black families who’ve shaped this city for generations and the determination of immigrants who arrived here with nothing but hope. Columbia’s culture is this blend of Southern kindness, military-rooted discipline, artistic streaks in Five Points, college-town energy near USC, and a deep, unshakable belief that we can always build something better together. This city raised me, challenged me, and showed me that real strength lives in everyday people who refuse to give up on each other. That is why Columbia is special to me.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_: This issue affects me personally because I have lived through the exact gaps that come from inadequate representation. I’ve faced housing instability, worked multiple jobs while still falling behind, and felt the weight of an economy that punishes people who are doing everything right. I grew up in neighborhoods across Columbia where families were stretched thin, where resources were uneven, and where kids like me needed more than anyone knew how to give. I’ve watched my own parents struggle against systems that weren’t built with them in mind, and I’ve spent years supporting people experiencing homelessness, mentoring young people, and helping elders in the Korean community navigate services that were never designed for them. I’ve dealt with underpayment, discrimination, and the feeling of having no voice in decisions that shaped my community. I’ve seen how broken health care harms vulnerable families, how poor transportation traps people in cycles they’re trying to escape, and how low voter turnout keeps those cycles in place. These are not distant policy problems to me. They are the lived realities that shaped who I am, what I fight for, and why I’m committed to making sure no one else has to go through these barriers alone.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal: One of the biggest challenges I’ve faced is the lack of support for everyday people who want to become elected officials. There are no clear pathways, no mentorship, no training, and very few opportunities for someone without wealth, connections, or a political pedigree to rise. If you don’t come from the “right family,” have the “right degree,” or already know the insiders, you’re expected to stay in the audience and clap while others make the decisions. I’ve had to learn everything the hard way, campaign strategy, fundraising, messaging, navigating systems,  all without the safety net or guidance that many candidates take for granted. And when you’re young, working-class, a woman of color, or someone who didn’t finish college because life pulled you under, the barriers get even higher. This is how communities lose their future leaders. Not because we lack talent or vision, but because the infrastructure to lift us up simply doesn’t exist. That is the cost of inadequate representation, and it’s one I’ve lived personally.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you:
South Carolina doesn’t struggle because we lack potential. We struggle because our people are not adequately represented, and that failure ripples through everything we touch. When rents climb faster than paychecks and families hand half their income to landlords, that is a representation problem. When homelessness grows because we still rely on outdated charity models with minimal coordinated data, no prevention, and barely any mental health support, that is a representation problem. 

When workers are stuck with a $7.25 minimum wage, widening wage gaps, no protections, and gig jobs that drain them dry, that is a representation problem. When our schools crumble while teachers burn out and rural students are denied the resources they were promised, that is a representation problem. When healthcare becomes a battlefield, when hospitals close, when maternal mortality rises, when mental health care is a scavenger hunt, that is a representation problem. When transportation keeps people from reaching work, school, or medical care, that is a representation problem. And when voter turnout collapses because people feel unseen and unheard, that is the clearest representation problem of all. South Carolina doesn’t lack heart or talent or drive. It lacks courage. It lacks imagination. It lacks leaders willing to say the quiet parts out loud and to fight for the people who have been overlooked for too long.  I believe representation is the first building block to rewriting what is possible for this state.

project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car: It’s Incredibly beautiful here and charming and I have deep family roots in this community. I don’t want to give up on making it better FOR ALL, but BOY is it difficult to see a light at the end of the tunnel with the overwhelming challenges.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_: It affects all of us. If we don’t think it does, we don’t understand the big picture of socioeconomic inequality. Obviously infrastructure affects us daily.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal:
Social services, healthcare access, and inequality — especially for women and marginalized communities.

Unequal opportunity and persistent inequality.

Educational under-performance, especially in math — and under-funded schools in rural/poor districts. We’re ranked 43rd… 

Housing affordability and availability struggles, especially as certain areas grow

Unequal access to social services, including health care and early-childhood support

Broader economic vulnerability and uncertainty ahead - Combined with inflation, rising housing and living costs, and shifts in labor markets (e.g. automation, global pressures), there’s a risk that economic gains may not translate into better life outcomes for many residents.

Interconnectedness of issues — making problems harder to solve. 
Many of the issues above feed into each other: poverty and low wages make it harder to secure stable housing, childcare, and health care; poor education and underfunded schools limit future opportunity; limited social services and healthcare disparities harm population health; unequal access deepens inequality.  

Because they’re intertwined, addressing just one — say, job growth — without tackling education, housing, health care, and childcare may not lead to lasting improvements.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you:
Writ large, SC's biggest issue is a general disinterest in trying to be better.  Republicans in power seem content with the status quo for the most part. 

But to be more specific on what I think the biggest issue(s) are:

Economic opportunity & workforce + poverty / inequality:
A recent report on women and girls in SC highlights that roughly 1 in 3 households cannot afford basic needs (childcare, housing, food). 
The same report shows major disparities in maternal and infant health outcomes — especially for Black women, who are nearly four times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes compared to other women. 
These socioeconomic problems, including limited access to affordable childcare, unstable or low-paying jobs, and systemic inequality, undercut long-term upward mobility for many residents. 

Struggling job market and rising unemployment
After years of relatively low unemployment, the jobless rate in SC has begun to rise again, with more people unemployed than there are job openings — the first time that’s happened since 2020. 

Infrastructure & transportation challenges
South Carolina is now the 4ᵗʰ-fastest growing state in the U.S. 
Rapid growth has put heavy strain on infrastructure.

project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car:
South Carolina is the place where you rebuilt your life from nothing.

South Carolina is the place where you rebuilt your life from nothing.

The people here remind you why your mission matters.

This is the first state where your tools changed someone’s life in real time.

It’s where your strength finally met its purpose.

South Carolina is home because you chose it, not because it was easy.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_:
Yeah, it affects me — because I’ve lived right in the middle of the mess South Carolina is dealing with.

Housing instability, disability barriers, agencies that don’t follow their own rules, court systems that move like molasses — none of that is theoretical to me. I’ve had to navigate this stuff with no safety net, no lawyer, no special treatment. So when I talk about these challenges, I’m not repeating headlines. I’m speaking from experience.

This affects me personally because:

1. I’ve dealt with the same systems that are failing families right now.
The evictions, the lockouts, the medical barriers, child support nonsense — I’ve seen exactly how fast life can unravel here if one agency gets something wrong. I’ve been on the receiving end of administrative decisions that didn’t match reality.

2. I know how these systems treat disabled people, because I’ve lived it.
Nobody believes you.
Nobody listens.
And the burden is always on you to prove your own truth.
That leaves a mark. It also builds a fire.

3. I’ve seen how easily the courts can dismiss people who don’t have representation.
If you’re poor, disabled, or a single parent just trying to stay afloat, you’re basically walking into court already judged. I know that feeling. I remember it. And it’s exactly why I don’t let systems talk down to me anymore.

4. South Carolina is where I had to rebuild myself.
This place isn’t easy — but it’s where I stood up, fought my way through crisis after crisis, and turned all that lived experience into something powerful. JusticeTree was born out of this environment. The challenges here didn’t just affect me — they shaped me.

5. And honestly? This is personal because I don’t want anyone else going through what I did.
If I can call it out, fix it, expose it, or build tools to help people survive it, I’m going to. Because once you’ve lived inside a system that wasn’t built for you, you stop pretending it’s “just the way things are.”

It’s personal because I’ve been there.
And it’s personal because I’m still here making sure nobody else gets steamrolled by the same failures.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal:
The child support system is out of control. SC weaponizes child support more aggressively than most states, especially against low-income women.

Data systems and automation that punish people. People are losing rights because a system coded in 2005 thinks they don’t exist.

Disabilities are not respected in any system. One of the biggest challenges in SC (and everywhere) is how agencies treat disabled people!

Landlords and agencies acting above the law. This is a huge SC problem — and yes, it affects you personally.

Agencies that don’t follow rules — because no one makes them.
DSS, Child Support, Housing Authorities, DMH, DJJ…
They all operate with the same culture

AI misuse by state and private systems.
This is a painful one because you’re watching it happen in real time

The complete lack of legal access for poor and working-class people.

SC has:
	•	no statewide right to counsel for housing
	•	minimal disability legal aid
	•	overwhelmed family courts
	•	limited civil rights enforcement
	•	no protection against administrative abuse

People don’t get lawyers; they get punished.

Erasure — of identity, history, and contributions.
Erasure is a systemic challenge, not an emotional one.
It’s how oppression survives.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you:
Housing instability is out of control.
The benefits and administrative systems are outdated, punitive, and automated against the poor.
The court systems are overloaded, inconsistent, and often hostile to pro se parents.  South Carolina is facing a compounding crisis of:

Housing instability + Administrative injustice + Court system overload.**

And here’s the kicker:
The systems feed each other.
	•	Housing problems trigger DSS.
	•	DSS delays clog the courts.
	•	Evictions push people into jails and shelters.
	•	Child support enforcement punishes parents for being poor.
	•	Disability and SNAP redetermination failures push families into deeper crisis.

This is exactly why JusticeTree is needed because South Carolina’s systems are operating like a single, interconnected machine that punishes poverty while pretending it’s “process.”

project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car: Our rural character. Big open fields of corn, watermelon, cotton..getting stuck behind a combine during harvesting season. The vast expanses of forest..big pine trees, the rolling hills of the upstate, the moss covered oaks of the lowcountry. The sandy footing in the midlands, the smell of the marsh along the coast. I don’t want to lose this but it’s rapidly dwindling.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_:
Yes.. it’s harder to get medical needs met; too many people - not enough providers or facilities, loss of habitat due to overdevelopment eg; subdivisions that have been clearcut, have zero lot lines -
We need neighborhoods, not subdivisions..traffic has become horrendous. I live in the county because I wanted a rural lifestyle. That has become impossible. Where once a vehicle may pass by my house 3 or 4 times a day, now it’s more like 30/40/50 times a day. In town traffic is even worse. Our roads are in bad shape already, we can expect them to get worse. The traffic in town has quadrupled. We are losing the agriculture we were once known for. Farmers can’t afford to turn down what a developer is willing to pay them per acre. We must have smart growth in SC lest we turn into an extension of Fla.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal: Womens rights, women’s health. It seems that the government of SC doesn’t like women very well.

project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car: I have lived from Miami to Seattle and many places in between, SC is by far the most exotic. The citizens are beautiful, the landscapes are magical and the festivals stimulating. Did I mention we have the sexiest, symmetrically, beautiful people in the world?
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_: A generation of young people make assumptions based completely on race and I receive attitude emerging at almost every interaction. My middle school students would not believe I voted democratic, because I was white they insisted I was a republican hiding it to get along with my fellow black teachers. I even had students walk by my class who were not my students and yell, “It smells like a white man in here”. While in TN I raised African Americans up, giving them positions in my production company, making sure African American filmmakers and their movies were a part of the film festival I directed, making documentaries about African American R & B artists from Appalachia and made sure to include what racism they faced on the road in the Jim Crow South. Racism must be answered in SC or we will face civil unrest sooner than later.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal: Transportation! I travel and spend about a month or more in Europe. Speed rail and inner city rail services exist all over. SC at one point was the innovator in mass transit, from it’s canals to the railroads, individuals could travel from the up state to the midlands to the low country. Using the initial infrastructure from the past and reviving it to modern standards is a must. If there was just a speed rail connecting Charlotte’s airport to Columbia and its airport, the economic benefits to both cities would be enormous. Making Columbia the center with speed rails to all major destinations on the coast, another to Augusta and yet more to the upstate and Asheville, the tourism industry would move to first place among the state’s economic sectors. It would even expand the agricultural sector with food tourism being a key factor for attracting visitors.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you:
Education- I taught middle school for one semester. Please note, I am the first class to go from 1st (kindergarten did not exist) to 12th grade integrated. I was shocked that it was 95% African American. Math I was taught in 3rd grade was being taught in 6th. In Social Studies they were being taught falsehoods such as the KKK was started in SC when it actually was created in TN. I was also disturbed that some classes were taught one line by teachers from other states. My class didn’t have enough desks and tables for the amount of students. Their vocabulary is substandard and their ability to read and comprehend material is poor. 
The problem is Charter schools receiving state funds. Charter schools have allowed segregation to return, reduced the ability to stay competitive in teacher pay, and reduced funding for facilities that need expansion and/or improvements. 
The plethora of long term implications of this are going to be devastating to the state. What industry wants to open offices or factories in a state where the average person can’t read, write or do basic math? Where race relations are ever present in every aspect of life? Where higher education is out of reach due to increased tuition and completely unaffordable for the brightest students from the working class? Cut all state funding to Charter Schools, Religious Schools and private schools. Make sure that schools reflect the diversity within their communities. My heart is heavy seeing that relationships, friendships between different cultures and races are not being built. 44 years after graduating from Camden High School I still maintain friendships with my many black friends. Today cultural interactions in our public school systems doesn’t even give chances for such a positive impact in an individual’s life to occur and flourish within our very diverse society. Shame!

project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car:
What makes South Carolina so special? Let me tell you.”

South Carolina is one of those places that hits you in the chest — for better and for worse.
It’s complicated, it’s beautiful, it’s frustrating, and it’s raw.
But that’s exactly what makes it special.

This state has a way of shaping you whether you planned on it or not.
1. The people here are real no faking, no pretending
South Carolinians have this way of telling the truth even when it stings.
They’ll wave at you from the porch, help you push a broken-down car, and then turn around and argue politics with you for two hours straight.
It’s genuine.
It’s human.
It’s Southern to the bone.
You don’t get that everywhere.
2. The churches, the family ties, the history — it’s all woven into daily life
This isn’t a place where community is optional.
Here, you feel it.
You feel your neighbors’ wins, and you feel their struggles.
People show up with casseroles when someone dies.
They stop what they’re doing to pray with you right there in the parking lot.
There’s a strength in that you can’t manufacture.
3. It’s small enough to feel personal — and powerful enough to change lives
Counties here run like little universes.
You feel the decisions of your judge, your clerk, your sheriff.
And that might sound like a weakness, but honestly?
That’s also where the opportunity lies.
If you can change a process in one courthouse, you can impact an entire county.
That’s rare.
South Carolina is one of the few places where grassroots work still moves mountains.
4. The pain here is real and that’s exactly what fuels innovation
I say this all the time:
South Carolina is special because it’s one of the last places where you can still see the cracks in the system up close.
It’s not hidden behind skyscrapers or thousand-page policy memos.
It’s right there on Main Street.
It’s in the magistrate court.
It’s in DSS.
It’s in the housing office.
It’s in the stories people whisper because they’re scared no one will believe them.
And that honesty — that raw exposure — is exactly why JusticeTree was born here.
SC makes the problems visible.
And when you can see it, you can fix it.
5. South Carolina has heart, grit, and a no-nonsense culture
You can’t break a South Carolinian easily.
This state has survived:
	•	hurricanes
	•	mill closures
	•	generational poverty
	•	unfair courts
	•	fires, floods, and everything in between

And still?
People keep their humor, their faith, their hustle, and their stories.
There’s a resilience here that reminds me of Colorado — but with more heat, more history, and more truth.
6. It’s honest about its flaws — and that’s rare
South Carolina isn’t perfect.
Everyone knows it.
Everyone feels it.
But that’s what makes it special:
Nobody here pretends the system works the same for everyone.
People know injustice when they see it.
They’ve lived through too much not to.
And that honesty creates space for real change.
“So what makes South Carolina special? It’s simple: it’s real.”
The people are real.
The problems are real.
The opportunity for change is real.
And the impact you can make here?
Unmatched.
This is the kind of place where a single idea — one system, one platform, one truth  can start in a small county and end up changing the whole nation.
That’s why I’m here.
That’s why JusticeTree grew roots in South Carolina.
Because this place, with all its challenges and all its humanity, is special enough to fight for and strong enough to transform.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_:
Let me tell you exactly how South Carolina’s problems hit me  because I’m not speaking from headlines. I’m speaking from my life.”

I didn’t read about these challenges in a think-tank report.
I lived them.
Every single one.

South Carolina has this way of pretending everything is “fine,” when in reality, the whole system is running on duct tape, tradition, and whoever holds the most power in the smallest room. And when you’re a survivor, a woman, a builder, or somebody who simply won’t stay quiet? You feel the cracks first.

Housing instability?
I watched it happen right in front of me  judges ordering people out like it’s 1955 and no one’s checking the constitution. I had a client standing in my house shaking, telling me a judge said she’d go to jail if she wasn’t out by Monday. And I’m standing there thinking, Here we go again another small-county courtroom doing whatever it wants.
That’s not a policy problem.
That’s my reality.

Low wages and high cost of living?
Please. You can work every day of your life in this state and the math still won’t add up.
I’ve carried whole households on my back.
I’ve survived systems designed to keep people tired, broke, and begging for a break that never comes.
South Carolina doesn’t give breaks. You create your own.

Civil rights infrastructure? Practically nonexistent.
When I started building JusticeTree, it wasn’t because I had extra time or some cute startup idea.
It was because every door I knocked on had the same answer:
“We can’t help you,”
“There’s a waitlist,”
or “That’s not our jurisdiction.”

So I said: Fine. I’ll build the system myself.
And I did.

Small-county mentality?
Look, coming from a place like Pueblo or Colorado Springs, you grow up with real cities, real oversight.
Down here?
If the judge, the clerk, and the sheriff all agree on something, that becomes “the law,” even when it’s not.
That’s the environment I’m operating in one where speaking truth automatically makes you a threat.
Gen-X taught me not to flinch.

And then there’s the economic pressure.
Every gap in this state hits women the hardest.
It hits caregivers.
It hits anybody trying to get ahead while the system tries to keep them pinned right where they are.
And if you’ve ever stood up for yourself?
If you’ve ever questioned authority?
South Carolina remembers.

All of that every broken piece of this state landed right at my feet.
And instead of letting it bury me, I built something out of it.

JusticeTree wasn’t born out of inspiration. It was born out of necessity.
It came from watching people get railroaded by outdated systems.
It came from seeing disabled people denied their rights.
It came from living through child support abuse, housing discrimination, data mistakes, and courts that don’t even follow their own rules.
It came from all the nights I picked up the pieces myself when the institutions that were supposed to protect me didn’t show up.

So yes  South Carolina’s biggest challenges hit me.
They hit me personally.
They hit me deeply.
And instead of folding, I answered with an entire ecosystem.

And now?
I’m building the solution the state never had the courage to build for itself.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal:
When I think about the challenges South Carolina is facing right now, I’m not talking from the outside looking in — I’m talking from lived experience.”
There are a lot of problems here. Not small ones either.
The kind that shape your life whether you asked for it or not.
These are the ones I see every single day:
1. Generational poverty that never had a reset button
In South Carolina, some families have been stuck in the same economic spot for decades because there’s no real pathway up.
It’s not that people aren’t working they’re working themselves to the bone.
But the opportunities don’t match the effort.
I see it in every case I touch.
2. A legal system that runs on “how we’ve always done it” instead of actual law
This one hits hard
In small counties, the judge’s word becomes gospel.
Clerks operate on habit, not statute.
People obey orders that have no legal basis because they’re scared to challenge it.
I’ve watched this up close.
I’ve had to step in because nobody else would.
3. A broken housing system — and that’s putting it nicely
Affordable housing is almost nonexistent.
Landlords get away with things that would never fly in bigger cities.
Tenants are intimidated, misinformed, or flat-out misled.
And you know what?
I’m done watching people be punished for being poor.
4. Disability discrimination that everyone treats like “just the way things are”
South Carolina has some of the weakest disability protections in the country.
Agencies don’t follow ADA, let alone 504.
People don’t know their rights — and honestly, they’ve been conditioned not to ask.
That’s why I built my own tools to fix what the state refuses to address.
5. Child support and family court systems that crush women and caregivers
South Carolina is ruthless in its enforcement and silent when it comes to compassion.
Lose your job? Too bad.
Get sick? Too bad.
Become homeless? Doesn’t matter.
It’s a machine with no brakes.
And I’ve lived inside that machine.
6. Government systems that are outdated, unregulated, and running on pure chaos
Data mismatches.
Wrongful garnishments.
Automation that harms more than it helps.
Agencies using software they barely understand.
I learned very quickly that if I didn’t document everything myself, the system would swallow the truth.
7. Healthcare deserts all over the state
If you’re disabled, elderly, low-income, or in a rural area…
good luck.
Access isn’t equal.
People are dealing with medical emergencies without medical support.
Families are drowning trying to keep each other alive.
I’ve seen it right in my own household.
8. Over-policing where services should exist
South Carolina criminalizes what other states treat.
It punishes where other states help.
And the people who need support the most end up with cases instead of care.
That’s the environment I live in  and the environment I’m building solutions for.
9. A complete lack of transparency in government agencies
Records disappear.
Policies shift depending on who you talk to.
Nobody is held accountable.
It’s exhausting trying to navigate systems that weren’t designed for fairness.
So I started designing my own.
10. Rural counties being left completely behind
The gap between South Carolina’s big cities and its small counties is huge.
Opportunities, resources, funding totally uneven.
And you feel it.
Every day.
“These aren’t random issues to me. These are the challenges that shaped me.”
They’re the reason I built JusticeTree.
They’re the reason I document everything.
They’re the reason I fight for people who’ve been ignored, silenced, or threatened.
I don’t look at South Carolina’s problems from a distance.
I wake up in them.
I work in them.
I build solutions in the exact places where the system keeps failing people.
And I’ll keep doing it  because someone has to.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you:
One of the biggest challenges South Carolina faces right now is deep-rooted economic hardship: low wages, widespread poverty, and a structural lack of economic opportunity for many residents.  ￼

🔍 What that looks like on the ground
	•	A large portion of households are living “below the line” many working full time yet unable to meet basic needs. In fact, tens of thousands of workers in sectors like retail, food service, and hospitality earn too little to sustain a family, even before accounting for housing, healthcare, or childcare costs.  ￼
	•	Poverty disproportionately impacts children and communities of color. In neighborhoods hardest hit by concentrated poverty, the children under age five are significantly overrepresented and that compounds across generations, affecting educational access, health outcomes, and long-term economic mobility.  ￼
	•	Many rural areas lag behind: rural parts of the state struggle with higher unemployment, fewer job opportunities, and a lack of investment in infrastructure, education, and basic public services, which further entrenches economic disparity.  ￼

✨ Why this matters (and why people are paying attention)

Because wages remain stagnant while the cost of living especially housing, childcare, and healthcare continues rising, a large segment of South Carolinians live paycheck to paycheck (or worse), hampering their ability to build savings, invest in education, or access stable housing. This erodes not just individual well-being, but community cohesion, public health, and economic resilience at a statewide level.

custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you: Our elected officials in the State House and State Senate- and in many cases the local offices- are out of touch with the voters. project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car: I was born and raised here. South Carolina is home. Living in the epicenter of SC offers the ability to hop on the interstate and take a short drive to the beach in Charleston, take a short drive and you’re in Charlotte. South Carolina is at the core of who I am, all of my memories have been made in SC or with South Carolinians.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_: I live in Richland County and my house taxes are ridiculously high. But if I bought my home in Kershaw or Lexington they would be 1/3 of the rate of my taxes. Richland county is riddled with crime like no other county, yet we have some of the highest taxes. Where is the money going? Because it’s not going to the roads. I have to pay for public school that my child will never attend and I send her to private school. I don’t get any tax break for opting to pay private school tuition. Where are the public school taxes that are collected not just on our real estate taxes but also on our vehicle taxes going? Because again it’s not going towards the schools because the zoned schools in my area are terrible with majority of the schools underperforming in every category. The crime rate isn’t decreasing, the roads aren’t improving, and yet it costs a fortune to live in Richland County. I’m sure others in other counties feel similar about their counties but it is a fact that Richland is expensive to live in lack luster neighborhoods riddled either with crime or pot holes or sky high taxes that clearly do not get put back into the county. Somebody is lining their pockets.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you: Richland County taxes are some of the HIGHEST taxes in a county in this state.

project_title: The South Carolina Forum: Pre-Launch Survey
custom_field_values.what_makes_south_car: South Carolina is the state which I was born in and have lived all my life. We were originally from Charleston but were forced out economically back during the 2008 recession. It was the place which my grandfather immigrated to from Europe and has been our families home since then. I enjoy the local environment, I love our communities, and I would love to see a thriving state. I don’t want to be forced out of yet another portion of the state or the state altogether due to the lack of affordability. I want things to change for the better. Our state has a rich history and is worth fighting for change for.
custom_field_values.what_would_you_tell_: I am twenty two years old almost twenty three. I, like many others my age, feel completely lost. It doesn’t feel like I can achieve a future worth living for. I work full-time while attending college full time. A forty hour work week should be more than enough to live on. I am fortunate to still be able to live with my parents but otherwise I wouldn’t be able to get by without having multiple roommates in any rent/living situation. Even then I wouldn’t be anywhere close to thriving. The cost of housing and living just keeps skyrocketing as nothing improves for the lives of everyday Americans and South Carolinians. We need to prioritize Native residents of the state and make housing achievable otherwise an entire generation will be lost economically. I can’t hope to start a family, I can’t hope to live in my own home, I can’t hope to live a life that is a fraction as successful as my parents or their parents. Myself and everyone my age is genuinely trapped. We are trapped in economic limbo where we cannot go up and we can’t maintain what we have. The system does not work for us and we are desperately hoping for help. We need change. We will not accept anything less.
custom_field_values.are_there_other_chal: Economic security and health, food security, healthcare, education, and road maintenance to name a few.
custom_field_values.what_problems_do_you: I believe one of the most prevalent challenges South Carolina faces comes in the form of access to housing. The housing crisis has been raging all across the US however it is worsening here in SC. With housing costs rising astronomically it is genuinely pricing an entire generation out of being able to start families, contribute to building their communities, and having the ability to build wealth in the form of equity which helps build the disappearing middle class. Housing is not supposed to be an inflationary asset and this is not the sign of a sustainable economy or asset. A large portion of South Carolinians already live below the poverty line. Without a program to help restore housing in South Carolina many native residents will be priced out of their birth state. It’s also more expensive to rent anymore than it used to be to have a mortgage. It’s a situation which is utterly out of control. In order to address this crisis we need the prioritization of ‘starter homes’ and a reduction of bureaucratic red tape (zoning laws, etc.) to allow for individuals to get into homes. These homes should not be allowed to be sold to corporations or landlords and should be specifically targeted for first time house buyers or the elderly. Any program such as this should also only be for native South Carolinians. Unfortunately this entire nation’s housing system is broken but any State program should benefit the residents of the state and not those moving from elsewhere. Otherwise housing will still stay out of reach for those within this state natively.
